$m\parallel$ tangent at $P$ means $(h/a^2,\ k/b^2)\parallel(x_1/a^2,\ y_1/b^2)$, i.e. $(h,k)\parallel(x_1,y_1)$: $Z$ lies on the line $CP$.

$\vec{SZ}=\left(\frac ae-ae,\ k\right)=\left(\frac{b^2}{ae},k\right)=b^2\left(\frac{h}{a^2},\frac{k}{b^2}\right)$ (as $h=\frac ae$ and $\frac{h}{a^2}=\frac{1}{ae}$), parallel to the normal vector of $m$.
So $SZ\perp m$, i.e. $SZ$ is the perpendicular from $S$ to the tangent at $P$ (it passes through $S$ and is perpendicular to the tangent's direction).
Hence the perpendicular from $S$ upon the tangent and the line $CP$ both pass through $Z$, a point of the directrix.

useful_results: The directrix $x=\frac ae$ is the polar of the focus $(ae,0)$; the foot of the perpendicular from a focus on a tangent lies on the auxiliary circle.
The pole of a line through the focus lies on the directrix and the line joining the focus to it is perpendicular to that line (focal property of poles).
The pole of a line parallel to the tangent at $P$ lies on the diameter $CP$ (conjugate-direction property).
Instance: for $\frac{x^2}{4}+y^2=1$ (so $ae=\sqrt3$, $\frac ae=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$) and $P(\sqrt2,\frac1{\sqrt2})$ the two lines meet at $x=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.

concepts: Tangent and normal at the end of the latus rectum of a hyperbola
Area of the triangle formed with the transverse axis
questions.question: Tangent and normal are drawn at the upper end $(x_1,y_1)$ of the latus rectum $P$ with $x_1>0$ and $y_1>0$, of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{12}=1$, intersecting the transverse axis at $T$ and $G$ respectively. Find the area of the triangle $PTG$.
questions.key_idea: At the end of the latus rectum $P=\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$ the tangent cuts the axis at $\left(\frac ae,0\right)$ and the normal at $(ae^3,0)$.
solution: (The hyperbola equation is not legible in the PDF; the working's $e^2=1+\cdot=4$ and $b^2=12$ give $\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{12}=1$, which reproduces the key $45$.) Here $a=2$, $b^2=12$, $e^2=1+\frac{b^2}{a^2}=4$, $e=2$.
$TG=ae^3-\frac ae=\frac{a(e^4-1)}{e}=\frac{2\cdot15}{2}=15$; the height of $P$ above the axis is $y_1=\frac{b^2}{a}=a(e^2-1)=6$.
Area of $\triangle PTG=\frac12\cdot TG\cdot y_1=\frac12\cdot15\cdot6=45$ (in general $\frac{a^2(e^4-1)(e^2-1)}{2e}$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's hyperbola equation and most working lines are grey boxes (missing images); visible are 'G: (ae^3, 0)', 'e^2 = 1 + ... = 4, e = 2, b^2 = 12' and the key 45. The hyperbola x^2/4 - y^2/12 = 1 was recovered from them and the working was written out (it reproduces 45).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the focal distances and the angle-bisector theorem: the tangent bisects $\angle SPS'$ internally and the normal bisects it externally, with $PS=\frac{b^2}{a}=6$ and $PS'=PS+2a=10$.
solution: For the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{12}=1$: foci $S(4,0),\ S'(-4,0)$. At the end of the latus rectum $PS=\frac{b^2}{a}=6$ and $PS'=PS+2a=10$.
The tangent at $P$ bisects $\angle SPS'$ internally: $\frac{ST}{TS'}=\frac{PS}{PS'}=\frac{6}{10}$, so $T$ divides $SS'$ in the ratio $3:5$: $T=4-\frac38\cdot8=1$.
The normal bisects the exterior angle: $\frac{GS}{GS'}=\frac{6}{10}$ with $G$ outside $SS'$ beyond $S$: $\frac{G-4}{G+4}=\frac35$, so $G=16$.

useful_results: For $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$: the latus rectum end is $\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$; the tangent there meets the transverse axis at $\left(\frac ae,0\right)$ and the normal at $(ae^3,0)$.
General tangent at $(x_1,y_1)$ meets the axis at $\left(\frac{a^2}{x_1},0\right)$; the normal meets it at $\left(\frac{(a^2+b^2)x_1}{a^2},0\right)=(e^2x_1,0)$.
For a hyperbola the tangent at $P$ bisects $\angle SPS'$ (internal) and the normal bisects the external angle; for an ellipse it is the other way round.
$PT\perp PG$, so the triangle $PTG$ is right-angled at $P$.

concepts: Tangents from an external point to a hyperbola (chord of contact)
Area of the triangle formed by the tangents and the chord of contact
questions.question: Find the equations of the tangents to the hyperbola $x^2-9y^2=9$ that are drawn from $(3,2)$. Find the area of the triangle that these tangents form with their chord of contact.
questions.key_idea: Chord of contact of $(3,2)$ is $x-6y=3$; solving it with the hyperbola gives the two points of contact.
solution: The chord of contact (C.O.C.) with respect to $P(3,2)$ is $T=0$: $3x-9\cdot2y=9$, i.e. $x-6y=3$ ....(1).
$y=0$ or $y=-\frac43$, giving $x=3$ or $x=-5$. The points of contact are $Q(3,0)$ and $R\left(-5,-\frac43\right)$.
The triangle $PQR$ has $P(3,2),Q(3,0),R\left(-5,-\frac43\right)$: base $PQ=2$ along $x=3$ and the horizontal distance of $R$ from $x=3$ is $8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the tangents with the slope form $y=mx+c$ and the condition $c^2=a^2m^2-b^2$; then get $R$ from the tangent.
solution: The hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{1}=1$: $a^2=9,\ b^2=1$. A tangent through $(3,2)$: $y=mx+2-3m$, so $c=2-3m$.
The tangent: $y-2=\frac{5}{12}(x-3)$, i.e. $5x-12y+9=0$. The second tangent is the vertical one, $x=3$ (slope $\to\infty$; it is the tangent at the vertex $(3,0)$).

Contact point on $5x-12y+9=0$: it touches at $R=\left(-\frac{a^2m}{c},-\frac{b^2}{c}\right)$ with $c=2-\frac54=\frac34$: $R=\left(-\frac{9\cdot5/12}{3/4},-\frac{1}{3/4}\right)=\left(-5,-\frac43\right)$.

useful_results: Chord of contact of $(h,k)$ w.r.t. $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$: $\frac{hx}{a^2}-\frac{ky}{b^2}=1$.
Line $y=mx+c$ touches $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ iff $c^2=a^2m^2-b^2$, at the point $\left(-\frac{a^2m}{c},-\frac{b^2}{c}\right)$.
A vertical (or horizontal) tangent is missed by the slope form: always test $x=h$ separately.

concepts: Normal at the end of the latus rectum of a hyperbola

questions.question: The normal to the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ drawn at an extremity of its latus rectum is parallel to an asymptote. Show that the eccentricity is equal to the square root of $\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.
questions.key_idea: At $\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$ the normal has slope $-\frac1e$; setting $\frac1e=\frac ba$ and $b^2=a^2(e^2-1)$ gives $e^4-e^2-1=0$.
solution: (The hyperbola equation and several lines of the PDF's working are not legible; the surviving lines are $b^2=a^2(e^2-1)$, 'Let $e^2=t$' and $t^2-t-1=0$.) The extremity of the latus rectum is $P\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$.
Normal at $(x_1,y_1)$: $\frac{a^2x}{x_1}+\frac{b^2y}{y_1}=a^2+b^2$, so its slope is $-\frac{a^2y_1}{b^2x_1}$. At $P$: slope $=-\frac{a^2\cdot b^2/a}{b^2\cdot ae}=-\frac1e$ ....(1).
It is parallel to an asymptote $y=\pm\frac bax$: $\frac1e=\frac ba$ in magnitude ....(2).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's hyperbola and most working lines are grey boxes (missing images); the visible fragments are b^2 = a^2(e^2-1), 'Let e^2 = t' and t^2 - t - 1 = 0. The solution was written out from the standard derivation (it reaches exactly that quadratic).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the asymptote angle as $\varphi$ with $e=\sec\varphi$; the normal slope $-\frac1e=-\cos\varphi$ must equal $-\tan\varphi$ in magnitude.
solution: Let the asymptote $y=\frac bax$ make an angle $\varphi$ with the transverse axis: $\tan\varphi=\frac ba$, so $e=\sqrt{1+\tan^2\varphi}=\sec\varphi$.

The normal at the latus-rectum end $P\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$ meets the axis at $G=(ae^3,0)$, so its slope is $\frac{0-b^2/a}{ae^3-ae}=-\frac{b^2}{a^2e(e^2-1)}=-\frac1e=-\cos\varphi$ (using $b^2=a^2(e^2-1)$).
Parallel to the asymptote: $\cos\varphi=\tan\varphi$, i.e. $\cos^2\varphi=\sin\varphi$, so $\sin^2\varphi+\sin\varphi-1=0$.

useful_results: For $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ the end of the latus rectum is $\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$; the normal there has slope $-\frac1e$ and the tangent has slope $e$.
The asymptotes are $y=\pm\frac bax$; with $\varphi$ their inclination, $e=\sec\varphi$ and $\frac ba=\tan\varphi$.
$e^4-e^2-1=0$ gives $e^2=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (the golden ratio $\phi$): the hyperbola with $e^2=\phi$ is the one whose latus-rectum normal is parallel to an asymptote.

concepts: Tangents to a circle and a hyperbola at points on a line through the origin

questions.question: A line through the origin meets the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$ at $P$ and the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=a^2$ at $Q$. If the locus of the point of intersection of the tangent at $P$ to the circle and the tangent at $Q$ to the hyperbola is the curve $a^4(x^2-a^2)+\lambda x^2y^4=0$, then find the value of $\lambda$.
questions.key_idea: With $y=mx$ the two tangents become $x+my=a\sqrt{1+m^2}$ and $x-my=a\sqrt{1-m^2}$; squaring and combining eliminates $m$.
solution: (The PDF's working is mostly grey boxes; it is written out here and ends at the legible line $(a^4+4y^4)x^2=a^6$.) Let the line be $y=mx$.
It meets the circle at $P=\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{1+m^2}},\frac{am}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}\right)$ and the hyperbola ($x^2(1-m^2)=a^2$) at $Q=\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{1-m^2}},\frac{am}{\sqrt{1-m^2}}\right)$.
Tangent at $P$ to the circle: $xx_P+yy_P=a^2$, i.e. $x+my=a\sqrt{1+m^2}$ ....(1).
Tangent at $Q$ to the hyperbola: $xx_Q-yy_Q=a^2$, i.e. $x-my=a\sqrt{1-m^2}$ ....(2).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working is grey boxes (missing images) except the last line (a^4 + 4y^4) x^2 = a^6; the full solution was written from scratch.
useful_results: Tangent to $x^2+y^2=a^2$ at $(x_1,y_1)$: $xx_1+yy_1=a^2$; tangent to $x^2-y^2=a^2$ at $(x_2,y_2)$: $xx_2-yy_2=a^2$.
A line through the origin $y=mx$ meets $x^2-y^2=a^2$ only if $|m|<1$; the points are $\frac{a}{\sqrt{1\mp m^2}}(1,m)$ for the hyperbola/circle.
To eliminate a parameter that appears only as $\sqrt{1\pm m^2}$: square, then add and subtract the two squares.
Check ($a=1$, $m=\frac12$): the tangents meet at $x=\frac{\sqrt5+\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.992$, $y=\frac{\sqrt5-\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.252$, and $x^2-1+4x^2y^4\approx-0.0158+0.0159\approx0$.

concepts: Pencil of conics and the focus-directrix property of a parabola
Sum of the focal distances of the intersection points
questions.question: The graphs of $x^2+y^2+6x-24y+72=0$ and $x^2-y^2+6x+16y-46=0$ intersect at four points. Compute the sum of the distances of these four points from the point $(-3,2)$.
questions.key_idea: Adding the two equations removes the $y^2$ terms and leaves a parabola with focus $(-3,2)$; the focal distance of each point is its $y$-coordinate.
solution: (1)$+$(2): $2x^2+12x-8y+26=0$, i.e. $x^2+6x-4y+13=0$, so $(x+3)^2=4(y-1)$ ....(3): a parabola with vertex $(-3,1)$ and $a=1$, so the focus is $(-3,2)$ and the directrix is $y=0$.
The four intersection points lie on this parabola, so the distance of each from the focus $(-3,2)$ equals its distance from the directrix: $y$.
For each of these $y$ values, (3) gives two values of $x$ ($y>1$), so the four points have $y$-coordinates $y_1,y_1,y_2,y_2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the parabola by $(-3+2t,\ 1+t^2)$; the focal distance is $1+t^2$ and substituting in the circle gives a quartic in $t$ whose root sum of squares is what we need.
solution: From $(x+3)^2=4(y-1)$ write $x=-3+2t$, $y=1+t^2$. The focus is $(-3,2)$ and the distance of the point from it is $y-0=1+t^2$.
Its four roots $t_i$ give the four intersection points; $t^2$ takes the two values $u_1,u_2$ with $u_1+u_2=18$, each for two values of $t$ ($\pm$). So $\sum t_i^2=2(u_1+u_2)=36$.

useful_results: Adding or subtracting two conics can remove the $y^2$ term, giving a parabola (a pencil of conics); look for a focus in the data (here the given point $(-3,2)$).
For a parabola, distance from the focus $=$ distance from the directrix; for $(x-h)^2=4a(y-k)$ the focal distance of a point is $y-k+a$.
Sum of the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points of a circle and a parabola with a vertical axis can be read from the resultant in $y$ (here $y^2-20y+59=0$, each root giving two points).
Check numerically: $y=10\pm\sqrt{41}$; the two $y$ values give $2(10+\sqrt{41})+2(10-\sqrt{41})=40$.

concepts: Confocal ellipse and hyperbola (eccentricities and focal semi-axes)

questions.question: An ellipse and a hyperbola have their principal axes along the coordinate axes and have common foci separated by a distance $2\sqrt{13}$; the difference of their focal semi axes is equal to $4$. If the ratio of their eccentricities is $\frac37$, find the equations of these curves.
questions.key_idea: Common foci mean $ae=AE=\sqrt{13}$, so the eccentricity ratio $\frac eE=\frac Aa=\frac37$ fixes the semi-axes.
solution: (In the PDF the distance between the foci is hidden by a grey box and the answers likewise; $2\sqrt{13}$ is the value that makes the problem consistent - see the note.) Let the ellipse have $a,b,e$ and the hyperbola $A,B,E$.
The difference of the focal semi-axes is $4$: $a-A=4$ ....(2); the ratio of eccentricities: $\frac eE=\frac37$, i.e. $\frac Aa=\frac37$ (from $ae=AE$) ....(1).
useful_results: Common foci $(\pm c,0)$: for the ellipse $a^2-b^2=c^2$, for the hyperbola $A^2+B^2=c^2$, and $ae=AE=c$.
For confocal conics the ratio of eccentricities equals the inverse ratio of the focal semi-axes: $\frac eE=\frac Aa$.
The data '$a-A=4$ and $\frac Aa=\frac37$' fix $a,A$ without knowing $c$; $c$ is needed only for $b,B$.
A confocal ellipse and hyperbola cut each other orthogonally.

concepts: Tangent to a hyperbola and the perpendicular from the centre
Power of a point with respect to a circle
questions.question: From the centre $C$ of the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=9$, $CM$ is drawn perpendicular to the tangent at any point of the curve, meeting the tangent at $M$ and the curve at $N$. Find the value of the product $(CM)(CN)$.
questions.key_idea: $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $PN$ (right angle at $M$) and $C,M,N$ are collinear, so $CM\cdot CN$ is the power of $C$ with respect to that circle.
solution: Its slope is $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$, so the perpendicular slope is $-\sin\theta$.
The line through $C$ perpendicular to (1): $y=mx+c$ with $m=-\sin\theta$, $c=0$: $x\sin\theta+y=0$ ....(2).
Solve (2) with $x^2-y^2=a^2$: $x^2-x^2\sin^2\theta=a^2$, so $x^2=a^2\sec^2\theta$ and $x=a\sec\theta$. Hence the point of the curve on this line is $N\equiv(a\sec\theta,\ -a\tan\theta)$.
$CM\perp$ tangent, so $\angle PMN=90^\circ$ and $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $PN$; $C,M,N$ are collinear, so $CN\cdot CM$ is the power of $C$ with respect to this circle.
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the point of the hyperbola 'M = (a sec t, -a tan t)', but in the question M is the foot on the tangent; the point on the curve is N. Relabelled (the argument and the answer 9 are unchanged).

alternate_solutions.idea: Polar form about the centre: the tangent at distance $p$ with normal direction $\varphi$ has $p^2=a^2\cos2\varphi$ and the curve in direction $\varphi$ has $r^2\cos2\varphi=a^2$.
solution: For $x^2-y^2=a^2$ the tangent with unit normal $(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$ is at distance $p$ from the centre with $p^2=a^2\cos^2\varphi-a^2\sin^2\varphi=a^2\cos2\varphi$ (tangency condition of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ with $b=a$).
$M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ on the tangent, so $CM=p$ and $M$ lies in the direction $\varphi$.
The curve in the direction $\varphi$: a point $r(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$ satisfies $r^2(\cos^2\varphi-\sin^2\varphi)=a^2$, so $CN^2=\frac{a^2}{\cos2\varphi}$.

useful_results: Tangent at the parametric point $(a\sec\theta,a\tan\theta)$ of $x^2-y^2=a^2$: $x\sec\theta-y\tan\theta=a$.
The point $N=(a\sec\theta,-a\tan\theta)$ is the reflection of $P$ in the transverse axis (the perpendicular from the centre to the tangent meets the curve there).

For $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$: $p^2=a^2\cos^2\varphi-b^2\sin^2\varphi$ (tangent at distance $p$) and $r^2\left(\frac{\cos^2\varphi}{a^2}-\frac{\sin^2\varphi}{b^2}\right)=1$ along the direction $\varphi$.
The product $CM\cdot CN$ is independent of $\theta$ here because the hyperbola is rectangular ($a=b$); for general $a\ne b$ it depends on the direction $\varphi$.

concepts: Hyperbola from the focus-directrix definition
Asymptotes of a hyperbola (condition for a pair of lines)
questions.question: A hyperbola has one focus at the origin and its eccentricity $=\sqrt2$, and one of its directrices is $x+y+1=0$. Find the equation of its asymptotes.
questions.key_idea: The focus-directrix property gives $x^2+y^2=(x+y+1)^2$; the asymptotes have the same second-degree part and the constant that makes the equation a pair of lines.
solution: (The eccentricity is hidden in the PDF; $e=\sqrt2$ is the value that gives its printed equation $x^2+y^2=(x+y+1)^2$.) For $S=(0,0)$, directrix $x+y+1=0$: $SP^2=e^2\cdot(\text{distance to the directrix})^2$, i.e. $x^2+y^2=2\cdot\frac{(x+y+1)^2}{2}$.
The asymptotes differ from the hyperbola only in the constant: $2xy+2x+2y+c=0$ is a pair of lines.
For a pair of straight lines the condition $abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2=0$ with $a=b=0$, $h=1$, $g=f=1$ gives $2-c=0$, so $c=2$.
Combined equation of the asymptotes: $2xy+2x+2y+2=0$, i.e. $xy+x+y+1=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A rectangular hyperbola ($e=\sqrt2$) has perpendicular asymptotes at $45^\circ$ to the transverse axis; locate the centre from the focus and directrix.
solution: $e=\sqrt2$: the hyperbola is rectangular, its asymptotes are perpendicular and make $45^\circ$ with the transverse axis.
The transverse axis passes through the focus $(0,0)$ and is perpendicular to the directrix $x+y+1=0$: it is $y=x$.
The distance from the focus to the directrix is $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=ae-\frac ae=\frac{a(e^2-1)}{e}=\frac{a}{\sqrt2}$, so $a=1$ and the focus-to-centre distance is $ae=\sqrt2$.
The centre lies on $y=x$ on the far side of the directrix from the focus: $C=-\sqrt2\cdot\frac{(1,1)}{\sqrt2}=(-1,-1)$.
The asymptotes pass through $(-1,-1)$ at $45^\circ$ to the line $y=x$, i.e. they are $y+1=0$ and $x+1=0$.

useful_results: Focus-directrix property: $SP^2=e^2\,(\text{distance of }P\text{ from the directrix})^2$; for a focus at the origin and directrix $lx+my+n=0$: $x^2+y^2=\frac{e^2(lx+my+n)^2}{l^2+m^2}$.
The asymptotes of a hyperbola $S=0$ are $S+k=0$ for the value of $k$ that makes the equation a pair of lines; the pair is obtained by changing only the constant term.
For $e=\sqrt2$ (rectangular hyperbola) the asymptotes are perpendicular.
Pair of lines: $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ is a pair iff $abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2=0$.

concepts: Chords of a rectangular hyperbola of constant length
Locus of the midpoint of a chord
questions.question: If a rectangular hyperbola has the equation $xy=c^2$, then the locus of the middle points of its chords of constant length $6$ is $(x^2+y^2)(xy-c^2)=\lambda xy$. Find the value of $\lambda$.
questions.key_idea: With end points $\left(ct_1,\frac c{t_1}\right),\left(ct_2,\frac{c}{t_2}\right)$ the midpoint gives $t_1t_2=\frac hk$, and the length condition becomes a relation in $h,k$.
solution: Let the end points of the chord be $\left(ct_1,\frac{c}{t_1}\right)$ and $\left(ct_2,\frac{c}{t_2}\right)$, with midpoint $(h,k)$.
Length of the chord is $6$: $c^2(t_1-t_2)^2+c^2\left(\frac1{t_1}-\frac1{t_2}\right)^2=36$, i.e. $c^2(t_1-t_2)^2\left(1+\frac{1}{t_1^2t_2^2}\right)=36$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the end points as $M\pm3(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ and use that both lie on $xy=c^2$; adding and subtracting gives the locus without parameters $t_1,t_2$.
solution: Let the midpoint be $M(h,k)$ and the chord direction $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$; the end points are $(h+3\cos\alpha,\ k+3\sin\alpha)$ and $(h-3\cos\alpha,\ k-3\sin\alpha)$ (half-length $3$).

useful_results: For $xy=c^2$ the point $\left(ct,\frac ct\right)$; chord through $t_1,t_2$ has midpoint $\left(\frac{c(t_1+t_2)}{2},\frac{c(t_1+t_2)}{2t_1t_2}\right)$.
Locus of midpoints of chords of constant length $2L$ of $xy=c^2$: $(x^2+y^2)(xy-c^2)=L^2xy$ (here $L=3$, $\lambda=L^2=9$).
Fixed-length chords: write end points as $M\pm L(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ and eliminate $\alpha$ by adding and subtracting the two conditions.
For chords of any conic through the midpoint $(h,k)$ the slope is fixed by $T=S_1$; here the slope of the chord is $-\frac kh$.

concepts: Normal to a hyperbola at a parametric point
Chord joining two points of a hyperbola in terms of $\theta,\phi$
questions.question: If a chord joining the points $P(a\sec\theta,a\tan\theta)$ and $Q(a\sec\phi,a\tan\phi)$ on the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=a^2$ is a normal to it at $P$, then show that $\tan\phi=\tan\theta\left(4\sec^2\theta-1\right)$.
questions.key_idea: Equate the slope of the chord $PQ$ with the slope $-\sin\theta$ of the normal at $P$ to get $\tan\phi+\sin\theta\sec\phi=2\tan\theta$, then use $\sec^2\phi-\tan^2\phi=1$.
solution: (The PDF's working is grey boxes; it is written out here from the method it states: slope of the chord $PQ$ = slope of the normal at $P$.) Tangent at $P$: $x\sec\theta-y\tan\theta=a$, slope $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$; so the normal at $P$ has slope $-\sin\theta$.
Slope of the chord $PQ$: $\frac{a\tan\phi-a\tan\theta}{a\sec\phi-a\sec\theta}$. Equating to $-\sin\theta$: $\tan\phi-\tan\theta=-\sin\theta(\sec\phi-\sec\theta)$.

One root is $\sec\phi=\sec\theta$ (the point $P$ itself). The product of the roots is $-\frac{4\tan^2\theta+1}{\cos^2\theta}$, so the other root is $\sec\phi=-\sec\theta\,(4\tan^2\theta+1)=-\sec\theta\,(4\sec^2\theta-3)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working is grey boxes (missing images); the solution was written from the method it names (slope of PQ = slope of the normal at P, then (2)^2 - (1)^2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rotate by $45^\circ$: $X=x+y,\ Y=x-y$ turns $x^2-y^2=a^2$ into a rectangular hyperbola $XY=a^2$, where the normal-chord relation is $t_1^3t_2=-1$.
solution: Put $X=x+y,\ Y=x-y$ (a rotation through $45^\circ$ with scaling), so the curve becomes $XY=a^2$ and normals stay normals. $P$ has $X=a(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)=at_1$ and $Y=a(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=\frac{a}{t_1}$, with $t_1=\sec\theta+\tan\theta$. Likewise $Q$ has $t_2=\sec\phi+\tan\phi$.
For $xy=c^2$ the tangent at $t$ is $x+t^2y=2ct$ (slope $-\frac1{t^2}$), so the normal at $t_1$ has slope $t_1^2$; the chord through $t_1,t_2$ has slope $-\frac{1}{t_1t_2}$.
The chord is the normal at $P$: $t_1^2=-\frac1{t_1t_2}$, so $t_2=-\frac{1}{t_1^3}$.

useful_results: Hyperbola $x^2-y^2=a^2$: point $(a\sec\theta,a\tan\theta)$; tangent $x\sec\theta-y\tan\theta=a$, slope $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$; normal slope $-\sin\theta$.
For $xy=c^2$, the normal at $t_1$ meets the curve again at $t_2$ with $t_1^3t_2=-1$.
$x^2-y^2=a^2$ and $XY=a^2$ ($X=x+y,\ Y=x-y$) are the same curve in a $45^\circ$ frame; $t=\sec\theta+\tan\theta$ links the two parametrisations.
Identities: $\left(\sec\theta+\tan\theta\right)\left(\sec\theta-\tan\theta\right)=1$, $t^3-\frac1{t^3}=\left(t-\frac1t\right)\left(\left(t+\frac1t\right)^2-1\right)$.

concepts: Tangent and normal at a point of a hyperbola
Perpendiculars from the foci on the normal (harmonic mean)
questions.question: Prove that the part of the tangent at any point of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ intercepted between the point of contact and the transverse axis is a harmonic mean between the lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the foci on the normal at the same point.
questions.answer: If $PT$ is the intercepted part and $p_1,p_2$ the focal perpendiculars on the normal, then $PT=\frac{2p_1p_2}{p_1+p_2}$
questions.key_idea: With $P(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$ both $PT$ and $\frac1{p_1}+\frac1{p_2}$ reduce to expressions in $W^2=a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2$, giving $\frac{2}{PT}=\frac1{p_1}+\frac1{p_2}$.
solution: (The PDF's working is grey boxes; it is written out here.) Let $P(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$ and $W^2=a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2$.
Tangent at $P$: $\frac{x\sec\theta}{a}-\frac{y\tan\theta}{b}=1$. It meets the transverse axis ($y=0$) at $T(a\cos\theta,0)$.
Perpendiculars from the foci $S(ae,0)$ and $S'(-ae,0)$ on the normal: $p_1=\frac{|a^2e\cos\theta-a^2e^2|}{D}=\frac{a^2e(e-\cos\theta)}{D}$ and $p_2=\frac{a^2e(e+\cos\theta)}{D}$ (as $e>1$).
Hence $PT=\frac{2p_1p_2}{p_1+p_2}$: the tangent segment $PT$ is the harmonic mean of $p_1$ and $p_2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working and its hyperbola equation are grey boxes (missing images); the statement uses the standard hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 and the proof was written from scratch.

alternate_solutions.idea: The tangent bisects $\angle SPS'$; the focal perpendiculars on the normal are $SP\cos\beta$ and $S'P\cos\beta$, and the bisector $PT$ has length $\frac{2\,SP\cdot S'P\cos\beta}{SP+S'P}$.
solution: For a hyperbola the tangent at $P$ bisects $\angle SPS'$ internally. Let $\angle SPS'=2\beta$, so the tangent makes the angle $\beta$ with each of $PS,\ PS'$.
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so it makes the angle $90^\circ-\beta$ with $PS$ and with $PS'$.
Perpendicular from $S$ on the normal: $p_1=SP\sin(90^\circ-\beta)=SP\cos\beta$; from $S'$: $p_2=S'P\cos\beta$.
In $\triangle SPS'$ the internal bisector $PT$ of the angle $2\beta$ has length $PT=\frac{2\cdot SP\cdot S'P\cdot\cos\beta}{SP+S'P}$.
So $PT$ is the harmonic mean of $p_1$ and $p_2$.

useful_results: Hyperbola: the tangent at $P$ bisects $\angle SPS'$ internally and the normal bisects the exterior angle. (Ellipse: the other way round.)

Length of the internal bisector from the vertex of angle $A$ in a triangle with adjacent sides $b,c$: $\ell=\frac{2bc\cos\frac A2}{b+c}$ - which says $\frac1\ell=\frac12\left(\frac1{b\cos(A/2)}+\frac1{c\cos(A/2)}\right)$.
For the tangent at $P(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$: it meets the axis at $T(a\cos\theta,0)$ and $PT=|\tan\theta|\sqrt{a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2}$.
Conversely, $PT=\frac{2p_1p_2}{p_1+p_2}$ also gives the length of the intercepted tangent from the two focal perpendiculars alone.

concepts: Tangent to a hyperbola and its asymptotes

questions.question: Ascertain the co-ordinates of the two points $Q$ and $R$, where the tangent to the hyperbola $4x^2-9y^2=180$ at the point $P(9,4)$ intersects the two asymptotes. Finally prove that $P$ is the middle point of $QR$. Also compute the area of the triangle $CQR$ where $C$ is the centre of the hyperbola.
questions.answer: $Q(3,-2)$, $R(15,10)$; $P$ is the midpoint of $QR$; area $=30$ sq. units
questions.key_idea: The tangent at $P$ is $x-y=5$; intersect it with the asymptotes $2x\mp3y=0$.
solution: (The hyperbola is not legible in the PDF; $4x^2-9y^2=180$, i.e. $\frac{x^2}{45}-\frac{y^2}{20}=1$, is the hyperbola through $P(9,4)$ whose tangent there is the printed $x-y=5$.) Tangent at $P(9,4)$: $4\cdot9x-9\cdot4y=180$, i.e. $x-y=5$ ....(1).
The asymptotes of $4x^2-9y^2=180$ are $4x^2-9y^2=0$, i.e. $2x-3y=0$ and $2x+3y=0$.
Area of $\triangle CQR$ with $C(0,0)$: $\frac12\left|x_Qy_R-x_Ry_Q\right|=\frac12\left|3\cdot10-15\cdot(-2)\right|=\frac12\cdot60=30$ square units.

alternate_solutions.idea: A tangent forms a triangle of constant area $ab$ with the asymptotes, and the point of contact bisects the intercepted part: check both with $P=(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$.
solution: Here $a^2=45,\ b^2=20$. For $P(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$ the tangent $\frac{x\sec\theta}{a}-\frac{y\tan\theta}{b}=1$ meets $y=\frac bax$ at $Q_1=\left(a(\sec\theta+\tan\theta),\ b(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)\right)$ and $y=-\frac bax$ at $Q_2=\left(a(\sec\theta-\tan\theta),\ -b(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)\right)$.
So the area is $30$ and $P$ is the midpoint of $QR$.

useful_results: For $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ the part of any tangent between the asymptotes is bisected at the point of contact.
The triangle formed by a tangent and the two asymptotes has constant area $ab$.
Asymptotes: replace the constant of the equation by $0$: $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=0$.

concepts: Tangent to a hyperbola and its asymptotes (locus of a midpoint)
Locus using parametric coordinates
questions.question: The tangent at $P$ on the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ meets one of the asymptotes in $Q$. If the locus of the mid-point of $PQ$ is a hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=\lambda$, find the value of $4\lambda$.
questions.key_idea: In the parametrisation $P(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$, $Q$ on $y=\frac bax$ is $\left(a(\sec\theta+\tan\theta),b(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)\right)$; the midpoint's coordinates give $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=\frac34$.
solution: (The PDF's hyperbola equations are grey boxes and no working is shown; the standard hyperbola and the locus form $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=\lambda$ are assumed, and the solution is written here.) Let $P=(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)$; tangent $\frac{x\sec\theta}{a}-\frac{y\tan\theta}{b}=1$.
The asymptote $y=\frac bax$: substitute: $\frac{x}{a}(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=1$, so $x=a(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)$ and $Q=\left(a(\sec\theta+\tan\theta),\ b(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)\right)$.
Midpoint of $PQ$ $=(h,k)$ with $h=\frac a2(2\sec\theta+\tan\theta)$ and $k=\frac b2(\sec\theta+2\tan\theta)$.
So the locus is $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=\frac34$ (the other asymptote gives the same locus), so $\lambda=\frac34$ and $4\lambda=3$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's hyperbola equations and the answer are grey boxes (missing images); the standard hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 and the locus form x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = lambda were assumed. The result 4*lambda = 3 was derived here and checked against both asymptotes.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use asymptote-coordinates $U=\frac xa+\frac yb$, $V=\frac xa-\frac yb$: the hyperbola is $UV=1$, the asymptotes are $U=0,\ V=0$, and midpoints are preserved by this linear map.
solution: $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=UV$, so the hyperbola becomes $UV=1$; the asymptotes become the axes $V=0$ and $U=0$.
Take $P=(t,\frac1t)$ in $(U,V)$. The tangent to $UV=1$ at $P$ is $\frac Ut+Vt=2$. It meets the asymptote $V=0$ at $U=2t$, i.e. $Q=(2t,0)$.

useful_results: In asymptote coordinates $U=\frac xa+\frac yb,\ V=\frac xa-\frac yb$, the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is $UV=1$ and every property of the rectangular hyperbola $XY=c^2$ carries over.
The tangent at a point meets the asymptotes at points which are at $2\times$ the point's coordinates, and the point is the midpoint of the intercepted part.
The midpoint of $PQ$ ($Q$ on one asymptote) traces $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=\frac34$; the locus of the midpoint of $QR$ ($Q,R$ on different asymptotes) is the hyperbola itself.
Linear changes of variables preserve midpoints, which makes locus problems on a hyperbola easy in its asymptote coordinates.

concepts: Hyperbola from its asymptotes (family $\text{pair of asymptotes}=\text{constant}$)

questions.question: If the lines $x+y+1=0$ and $2x-y+2=0$ are the asymptotes of a hyperbola, and the line $x-2=0$ touches the hyperbola, then the equation of the hyperbola is $4(x+y+1)(2x-y+2)=\lambda$. Find the value of $\lambda$.
questions.key_idea: A hyperbola with these asymptotes is $(x+y+1)(2x-y+2)=c$; tangency of $x=2$ means equal roots in $y$.
solution: The hyperbola with the given asymptotes is $(x+y+1)(2x-y+2)=c$.
The line touches the hyperbola, so $D=0$: $9-4(c-18)=0$, giving $c=\frac{81}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The point of contact bisects the part of a tangent between the asymptotes: find the contact point on $x=2$ as the midpoint and substitute.
solution: The tangent $x=2$ meets the asymptote $x+y+1=0$ at $y=-3$ and the asymptote $2x-y+2=0$ at $y=6$.
The point of contact is the midpoint of this intercept: $\left(2,\frac{-3+6}{2}\right)=\left(2,\frac32\right)$.

useful_results: Any hyperbola with asymptotes $L_1=0,\ L_2=0$ is $L_1L_2=c$ (a one-parameter family); a point on it fixes $c$.
The part of any tangent intercepted between the asymptotes is bisected at the point of contact.
A line is tangent to $L_1L_2=c$ iff the quadratic obtained by substituting it has a zero discriminant.
Check: $c=\frac{81}{4}$ gives a double root $y=\frac32$ in $y^2-3y+\frac94=\left(y-\frac32\right)^2$.

concepts: Line of fixed gradient through a point of a hyperbola meeting its asymptotes
Product of segments (QP)(PR)
questions.question: Through any point $P$ of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ a line $QPR$ is drawn with a fixed gradient $m$, meeting the asymptotes in $Q$ and $R$. Show that the product $(QP)(PR)$ is constant, equal to $\frac{a^2b^2(1+m^2)}{|b^2-a^2m^2|}$.
questions.key_idea: Take the points of the line as $P+r(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ with $\tan\alpha=m$; substituting into the pair of asymptotes gives a quadratic in $r$ whose constant term is $1$ because $P$ is on the hyperbola.
solution: (The PDF's hyperbola, answer and working are grey boxes; the standard hyperbola is used and the result derived here.) Let $P=(x_0,y_0)$ with $\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}-\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}=1$. The line of gradient $m=\tan\alpha$: $(x,y)=(x_0+r\cos\alpha,\ y_0+r\sin\alpha)$, where $|r|$ is the distance from $P$.
The two roots $r_1,r_2$ are the signed distances $PQ,PR$: $r_1r_2=\frac{1}{\frac{\cos^2\alpha}{a^2}-\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{b^2}}=\frac{a^2b^2}{b^2\cos^2\alpha-a^2\sin^2\alpha}$.
So $(QP)(PR)=|r_1r_2|=\frac{a^2b^2(1+m^2)}{|b^2-a^2m^2|}$, which does not depend on $P$ (only on the fixed gradient $m$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's hyperbola, the required product and the whole working are grey boxes (missing images). The standard hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 was assumed and the product was derived here.

alternate_solutions.idea: In asymptote coordinates $U=\frac xa+\frac yb$, $V=\frac xa-\frac yb$ the hyperbola is $UV=1$ and the asymptotes are the axes; then $QP\cdot PR$ is read off from $U_0V_0=1$.
solution: In $(U,V)$ the hyperbola is $UV=1$ and the asymptotes are $V=0$ (through $R$, say) and $U=0$ (through $Q$). Let $P=(U_0,V_0)$ with $U_0V_0=1$.
Moving along the line by $dx=1,\ dy=m$ changes $(U,V)$ by $(dU,dV)=\left(\frac1a+\frac mb,\ \frac1a-\frac mb\right)$ and the actual length by $\sqrt{1+m^2}$.
The points $P+\lambda(dU,dV)$: $R$ at $V=0$ has $\lambda_R=-\frac{V_0}{dV}$ and $Q$ at $U=0$ has $\lambda_Q=-\frac{U_0}{dU}$.

useful_results: For a line through $P$ meeting a pair of lines $S_0=0$ at $Q,R$, the product $PQ\cdot PR=\frac{S_0(P)}{\text{(quadratic part of }S_0\text{ along the direction)}}$ - here $S_0(P)=1$ because $P$ is on the hyperbola.
For the horizontal direction ($m=0$) the product is $a^2$; for the vertical one it is $-b^2$ (opposite sides).
For a rectangular hyperbola $xy=c^2$ and a line through $P$ with gradient $m$: $PQ\cdot PR=c^2\cdot\frac{1+m^2}{|m|}$.
Check with $m=0$: $QP\cdot PR=a^2$ (the product of the horizontal distances from $P$ to $x=\pm\frac ab y_0$: $x_0^2-\frac{a^2y_0^2}{b^2}=a^2$).

concepts: Focal distance and directrix of a parabola
Equilateral triangle (area)
questions.question: A point $P$ on a parabola $y^2=4x$, the foot of the perpendicular from it upon the directrix, and the focus are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Find the area of the equilateral triangle.
questions.key_idea: For $P(t^2,2t)$, $PM=PS=1+t^2$ (focal distance), and $MS=2\sqrt{1+t^2}$; equilateral means $MS=PM$.
solution: Let $P=(t^2,2t)$ on $y^2=4x$; the focus is $S(1,0)$ and the directrix $x=-1$, so $M=(-1,2t)$.
$PM=t^2+1=1+t^2$ and $PS=1+t^2$ (focal distance equals the distance from the directrix).

alternate_solutions.idea: The side $MP$ is horizontal, so $MS$ must make $60^\circ$ with the horizontal: its slope is $\pm\sqrt3$.
solution: In the equilateral triangle $PMS$ the angle at $M$ is $60^\circ$, so the line $MS$ makes $60^\circ$ with the $x$-axis: its slope is $\pm\sqrt3$.

useful_results: Focus-directrix property of $y^2=4ax$: $PS=PM=a+x_P$; for $P(at^2,2at)$, $PS=a(1+t^2)$.
The triangle $PMS$ (foot of the directrix, point, focus) is isosceles with $PS=PM$ and equilateral iff the angle at $P$ is $60^\circ$, i.e. $t^2=3$.
The line $MS$ from the foot on the directrix to the focus has slope $-\frac{y_P}{2a}=-t$; the angle at $M$ is $\arctan|t|$.
Area of an equilateral triangle of side $s$: $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$.

concepts: Parabola through two points with a variable tangent to a circle as directrix (locus of the focus)
Latus rectum and tangents at its ends (area of the quadrilateral)
questions.question: Consider two concentric circles $S_1:|z|=1$ and $S_2:|z|=2$ on the Argand plane. A variable parabola is drawn through the points where $S_1$ meets the real axis and having an arbitrary tangent drawn to $S_2$ as its directrix. If the locus of the focus of the parabola is a conic $C$, then find the area of the quadrilateral formed by the tangents at the ends of the latus-rectum of conic $C$.
questions.key_idea: The distances of $(\pm1,0)$ from the focus equal their distances from the directrix: $2-\cos\theta$ and $2+\cos\theta$, whose sum is $4$: the focus lies on an ellipse with foci $(\pm1,0)$.
solution: The parabola passes through $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$. Let its directrix be the tangent $x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=2$ to $S_2$, and let $M(h,k)$ be the focus.
The distance of $(\pm1,0)$ from $M$ equals its distance from the directrix: $(h-1)^2+k^2=(\cos\theta-2)^2$ ....(1) and $(h+1)^2+k^2=(\cos\theta+2)^2$ ....(2).
The locus of the focus is $\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{3}=1$ (an ellipse) with $a=2$, $b^2=3$, $e^2=1-\frac34=\frac14$, so $e=\frac12$.

The tangents at the ends of the latus rectum $\left(\pm ae,\pm\frac{b^2}{a}\right)=\left(\pm1,\pm\frac32\right)$ are $x\pm2y=\pm4$; they meet the major axis at $\left(\pm\frac ae,0\right)=(\pm4,0)$ and the minor axis at $(0,\pm a)=(0,\pm2)$.
They form a rhombus with diagonals $\frac{2a}{e}=8$ and $2a=4$: area $=\frac12\cdot8\cdot4=\frac{2a^2}{e}=16$ square units.

alternate_solutions.idea: The distances of $A(1,0)$ and $B(-1,0)$ from the tangent line are $2-\cos\theta$ and $2+\cos\theta$; since $MA$ and $MB$ equal them, $MA+MB=4$ at once.
solution: The directrix $x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=2$ is at the signed distances $2-\cos\theta$ from $A(1,0)$ and $2+\cos\theta$ from $B(-1,0)$ (both on the same side).
$A,B$ lie on the parabola, so $MA=2-\cos\theta$ and $MB=2+\cos\theta$ ($M$ is the focus).
$MA+MB=4$, a constant larger than $AB=2$: $M$ lies on the ellipse with foci $(\pm1,0)$ and $2a=4$.

useful_results: If $A,B$ lie on a parabola with focus $M$ and directrix $\ell$, then $MA=d(A,\ell)$ and $MB=d(B,\ell)$.
For a tangent to a circle of radius $R$ about the origin ($x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=R$) the distances of $(\pm c,0)$ are $R\mp c\cos\theta$, with sum $2R$.
The tangents at the ends of the latera recta of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ form a rhombus with diagonals $\frac{2a}{e}$ and $2a$: area $\frac{2a^2}{e}$.
The tangent at $\left(ae,\frac{b^2}{a}\right)$ is $\frac{ex}{a}+\frac{y}{a}=1$, meeting the axes at $\left(\frac ae,0\right)$ and $(0,a)$.

concepts: Normals to a parabola from a point (slope form)
Locus of a point from a relation between slopes
questions.paragraph: From a point $P$ three normals are drawn to the parabola $y^2=4x$ such that two of them make angles with the abscissa axis, the product of whose tangents is $2$. Suppose the locus of the point $P$ is a part of a conic $C$. Now a circle $S=0$ is described on the chord of the conic $C$ as diameter passing through the point $(1,0)$ and with gradient unity. Suppose $(a,b)$ are the coordinates of the centre of this circle. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the two asymptotes of the hyperbola with length of its transverse axis $2a$ and $2b$ (principal axes of the hyperbola along the coordinate axes), then answer the following questions.
questions.question: Locus of $P$ is a:
questions.key_idea: The slopes of the three normals are the roots of $m^3+(2-h)m+k=0$; $m_1m_2=2$ fixes $m_3=-\frac k2$, and substituting gives $k^2=4h$.
solution: The normal of slope $m$ to $y^2=4x$ is $y=mx-2m-m^3$. Through $P(h,k)$: $m^3+(2-h)m+k=0$ ....(1).
Let the roots be $m_1,m_2,m_3$. Then $m_1m_2m_3=-k$. Given $m_1m_2=2$: $m_3=-\frac{k}{2}$.
The locus of $P$ is $y^2=4x$, a parabola. Answer (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's line 'k^3 - 4k(2-h) + 8k = 0' has the signs of the last two terms reversed (the correct equation is k^3 + 4k(2-h) - 8k = 0, i.e. after dividing by k, k^2 + 4(2-h) - 8 = 0), and its next line 'k^2 - 8 - 4h + 8 = 0' is not the expansion of either; only the final y^2 = 4x is right. Redone from m3 = -k/2.

alternate_solutions.idea: Normals at the feet $t_1,t_2$ meet on the parabola exactly when $t_1t_2=2$ (slopes $m_i=-t_i$), and the intersection point then satisfies $y^2=4x$.
solution: For $y^2=4x$ the normal at $t$ has slope $m=-t$, so $m_1m_2=2$ means $t_1t_2=2$.

useful_results: Normals at the feet $t_1,t_2$ of $y^2=4ax$ meet at $\left(a(t_1^2+t_2^2+t_1t_2+2),\ -at_1t_2(t_1+t_2)\right)$.
Normals at $t_1,t_2$ meet on the parabola iff $t_1t_2=2$.
Slope form: from $(h,k)$ the three normal slopes satisfy $m_1+m_2+m_3=0$, $\sum m_im_j=2a-h$, $m_1m_2m_3=-k$.
The locus of a point whose two normals have slope product $\alpha$ is $y^2=\alpha^2x+\alpha^3-2\alpha^2$ (for $y^2=4x$); $\alpha=2$ gives $y^2=4x$.

concepts: Focal chord of a parabola (parameters $t_1+t_2$, $t_1t_2$)
Circle on a chord as diameter
questions.paragraph: From a point $P$ three normals are drawn to the parabola $y^2=4x$ such that two of them make angles with the abscissa axis, the product of whose tangents is $2$. Suppose the locus of the point $P$ is a part of a conic $C$. Now a circle $S=0$ is described on the chord of the conic $C$ as diameter passing through the point $(1,0)$ and with gradient unity. Suppose $(a,b)$ are the coordinates of the centre of this circle. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the two asymptotes of the hyperbola with length of its transverse axis $2a$ and $2b$ (principal axes of the hyperbola along the coordinate axes), then answer the following questions.
questions.question: Radius of the circle $S=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: The chord through $(1,0)$ is a focal chord with slope $1$: $t_1+t_2=2$, $t_1t_2=-1$; the circle on it as diameter is $x^2+y^2-6x-4y-3=0$.
solution: The chord of $C:\ y^2=4x$ through $(1,0)$ passes through the focus, so it is a focal chord with end points $(t_1^2,2t_1),(t_2^2,2t_2)$ and $t_1t_2=-1$.
$S:\ x^2+y^2-6x-4y-3=0$; the centre is $(a,b)=(3,2)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{9+4+3}=4$. Answer (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: The centre is the midpoint of the focal chord, and the length of a focal chord inclined at $\theta$ is $\frac{4a}{\sin^2\theta}$.
solution: The focal chord has slope $1$ through $(1,0)$: $y=x-1$. With $y^2=4x$: $(x-1)^2=4x$, i.e. $x^2-6x+1=0$.
Length of a focal chord of $y^2=4ax$ inclined at $\theta$ to the axis is $\frac{4a}{\sin^2\theta}=\frac{4}{\sin^245^\circ}=8$ ($a=1$).

useful_results: A focal chord of $y^2=4ax$ joins the parameters $t$ and $-\frac1t$; its slope is $\frac{2t}{t^2-1}$ and its length is $a\left(t+\frac1t\right)^2$.
Length of a focal chord inclined at $\theta$ to the axis: $\frac{4a}{\sin^2\theta}$ (least $4a$ at $\theta=90^\circ$, the latus rectum).
Circle with diameter joining $(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)$: $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$.
The centre of the circle on a focal chord as diameter is the midpoint of the chord: here $\left(a(t_1^2+t_2^2)/2,\ a(t_1+t_2)\right)=(3,2)$.

Inverse tangent bounds
questions.paragraph: From a point $P$ three normals are drawn to the parabola $y^2=4x$ such that two of them make angles with the abscissa axis, the product of whose tangents is $2$. Suppose the locus of the point $P$ is a part of a conic $C$. Now a circle $S=0$ is described on the chord of the conic $C$ as diameter passing through the point $(1,0)$ and with gradient unity. Suppose $(a,b)$ are the coordinates of the centre of this circle. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the two asymptotes of the hyperbola with length of its transverse axis $2a$ and $2b$ (principal axes of the hyperbola along the coordinate axes), then answer the following questions.
questions.question: The angle $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ between the two asymptotes of the hyperbola lies in the interval:
questions.key_idea: The hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=1$; each asymptote has $\tan\theta=\frac23$ and $\alpha=2\theta$, so $\tan\alpha=\frac{12}{5}$.
solution: From the previous part the centre is $(a,b)=(3,2)$. The hyperbola has transverse axis $2a=6$ and conjugate axis $2b=4$: $\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=1$.
Its asymptotes are $y=\pm\frac23x$. Let each make an angle $\theta$ with the transverse axis: $\tan\theta=\frac23$.
The (acute) angle between the asymptotes is $\alpha=2\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cos\alpha=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2}=\frac{5}{13}$ and compare with $\cos75^\circ$ and $\cos60^\circ$.
solution: The angle between the asymptotes $y=\pm\frac baX$ satisfies $\cos\alpha=\frac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2}$ with $a=3,b=2$.

useful_results: Asymptotes of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$: $y=\pm\frac bax$; the angle between them is $2\tan^{-1}\frac ba$ (acute if $b<a$).
$\tan\alpha=\frac{2ab}{a^2-b^2}$ and $\cos\alpha=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2}$ for $\alpha=2\tan^{-1}\frac ba$.
Bounds: $\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$, $\tan75^\circ=2+\sqrt3$; $\cos75^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$.
The asymptotes are perpendicular iff $a=b$ (rectangular hyperbola), where $\cos\alpha=0$.

concepts: Differential equation from a bisected tangent intercept
Rectangular hyperbola $xy=c^2$ (vertices)
questions.paragraph: A conic $C$ passes through the point $(2,4)$ and is such that the segment of any of its tangents at any point contained between the co-ordinate axes is bisected at the point of tangency. Let $S$ denote the circle described on the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$ of the conic $C$ as diameter.
questions.question: Vertex of the conic $C$ is:
questions.key_idea: Bisection of the intercept at the point of contact gives $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac yx$, so $xy=c$; through $(2,4)$: $xy=8$.
solution: Let the tangent at $P(x,y)$ be $Y-y=m(X-x)$ with $m=\frac{dy}{dx}$.
$P$ bisects the intercepted segment: $x=\frac12\left(x-\frac ym\right)$, i.e. $x-\frac ym=2x$, so $-\frac ym=x$; and $y=\frac12(y-mx)$, i.e. $-mx=y$. Both give $m=-\frac yx$.
The curve passes through $(2,4)$: $c=8$. The conic is $xy=8$, a rectangular hyperbola with $e=\sqrt2$.
Its transverse axis is $y=x$, so the vertices are where $y=x$ meets it: $x^2=8$, i.e. $\left(2\sqrt2,2\sqrt2\right)$ and $\left(-2\sqrt2,-2\sqrt2\right)$. Answer (B).
questions.correction_note: Several lines and options (B), (D) are grey boxes in the PDF; the working above is the PDF's visible method with the hidden lines restored. Option (B) is reconstructed as the vertices of xy = 8 (consistent with the key B); option (D) is not recoverable.

alternate_solutions.idea: The vertices are the points of the curve nearest to the centre; minimise $x^2+y^2$ on $xy=8$ by AM-GM.
solution: The conic is $xy=8$. The vertices of a hyperbola are the points of the curve at the least distance from the centre (on the transverse axis).
By AM-GM: $x^2+y^2\ge2|xy|=16$, with equality iff $|x|=|y|$, i.e. $x=y$ (as $xy>0$).

useful_results: If the part of any tangent between the axes is bisected at the point of contact, the curve is a rectangular hyperbola $xy=c$ (since $d(xy)=0$).
For $xy=c^2$: the tangent at $\left(ct,\frac ct\right)$ is $x+t^2y=2ct$, with intercepts $2ct$ and $\frac{2c}{t}$ - the midpoint is the point of contact.

Rectangular hyperbola $xy=c^2$: $e=\sqrt2$, $a=\sqrt2c$, vertices $(\pm c,\pm c)$, foci $(\pm\sqrt2c,\pm\sqrt2c)$, directrices $x+y=\pm\sqrt2c$. (Here $c^2=8$: vertices $(\pm2\sqrt2,\pm2\sqrt2)$, foci $(\pm4,\pm4)$.)
Nearest points of a curve to the centre are found by minimising $x^2+y^2$ (AM-GM for $xy=c^2$).

questions.paragraph: A conic $C$ passes through the point $(2,4)$ and is such that the segment of any of its tangents at any point contained between the co-ordinate axes is bisected at the point of tangency. Let $S$ denote the circle described on the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$ of the conic $C$ as diameter.
questions.question: Director circle of the conic is:
questions.key_idea: For $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ the director circle is $x^2+y^2=a^2-b^2$; for the rectangular hyperbola $a=b$ this is the point circle $x^2+y^2=0$.
solution: The conic is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=8$ (equivalently $\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1$ in its axes), with $a=b=4$.
The director circle (locus of points from which perpendicular tangents are drawn) of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is $x^2+y^2=a^2-b^2$.
Here $a^2-b^2=0$, so the director circle is $x^2+y^2=0$: only the centre (a point circle, no real circle).
None of $x^2+y^2=4,\ 8,\ 2$ is this, so the answer is (D) None.

alternate_solutions.idea: From $(h,k)$ the pair of tangents to $xy=8$ is $S\cdot S_{11}=T^2$; the tangents are perpendicular iff the coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$ add to zero.
solution: For $S\equiv xy-8$, $S_{11}=hk-8$ and $T\equiv\frac{hy+kx}{2}-8$. The pair of tangents from $(h,k)$ is $(xy-8)(hk-8)=\left(\frac{hy+kx}{2}-8\right)^2$.
Coefficient of $x^2$: $-\frac{k^2}{4}$; coefficient of $y^2$: $-\frac{h^2}{4}$ (the left side has no square terms).
Only $(0,0)$ satisfies this (and the tangents from the centre are the asymptotes, which are perpendicular): the director circle degenerates to a point. Answer (D).

useful_results: Director circle of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is $x^2+y^2=a^2+b^2$; of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ it is $x^2+y^2=a^2-b^2$ (real only if $a>b$).
Rectangular hyperbola ($a=b$): the director circle is a point circle (the centre); no pair of tangents is perpendicular except the asymptotes.
For $y^2=4ax$ the director circle degenerates to the directrix.
Pair of tangents from $(h,k)$: $S\cdot S_{11}=T^2$; perpendicular iff $\text{coeff}(x^2)+\text{coeff}(y^2)=0$.

concepts: Foci of a rectangular hyperbola

questions.paragraph: A conic $C$ passes through the point $(2,4)$ and is such that the segment of any of its tangents at any point contained between the co-ordinate axes is bisected at the point of tangency. Let $S$ denote the circle described on the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$ of the conic $C$ as diameter.
questions.question: Equation of the circle $S$ is:
questions.key_idea: For $xy=8$ the foci are $(4,4),(-4,-4)$, so $S$ has centre the origin and radius $4\sqrt2$.
solution: The conic is $xy=8$, a rectangular hyperbola with $e=\sqrt2$ and vertices $\left(\pm2\sqrt2,\pm2\sqrt2\right)$ (previous parts), so $a=\sqrt{8+8}=4$.
The foci are at distance $ae=4\sqrt2$ from the centre along $y=x$: $F_1(4,4)$ and $F_2(-4,-4)$.
The circle $S$ on $F_1F_2$ as diameter has centre $(0,0)$ and radius $\frac{F_1F_2}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{64+64}}{2}=4\sqrt2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For $xy=c^2$ the foci are $(\pm\sqrt2c,\pm\sqrt2c)$; with $c^2=8$ the circle on them as diameter has radius $\sqrt2\cdot c\cdot\sqrt2=2c=4\sqrt2$.
solution: For $xy=c^2$, the focus $(f,f)$ satisfies $f^2=2c^2$ (focal property, equivalent to $ae=\sqrt2\cdot a$ with $a=\sqrt2c$).
The circle on them as diameter: centre $(0,0)$ and $r^2=f^2+f^2=32$. Answer (C): $x^2+y^2=32$.

useful_results: Rectangular hyperbola $xy=c^2$: foci $(\pm\sqrt2c,\pm\sqrt2c)$ (same sign), centre at the origin, $a=b=\sqrt2c$, $e=\sqrt2$.
Circle on the foci as diameter: $x^2+y^2=(ae)^2=2a^2=4c^2$ (here $4\cdot8=32$).
The distance between the foci of $xy=c^2$ is $4c$ (here $c=2\sqrt2$, so $F_1F_2=8\sqrt2$ and the radius is $4\sqrt2$).
For a general hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ the circle on the foci as diameter is $x^2+y^2=a^2+b^2$.

questions.question:
Consider the parabola $y^2=12x$:
Column I
(A) Tangent and normal at the extremities of the latus rectum intersect the $x$-axis at $T$ and $G$ respectively. The coordinates of the middle point of $T$ and $G$ are
(B) Variable chords of the parabola passing through a fixed point $K$ on the axis, such that the sum of the squares of the reciprocals of the two parts of the chords through $K$ is a constant. The coordinates of the point $K$ are
(C) All variable chords of the parabola subtending a right angle at the origin are concurrent at the point
(D) $AB$ and $CD$ are the chords of the parabola which intersect at a point $E$ on the axis. The radical axis of the two circles described on $AB$ and $CD$ as diameter always passes through
Column II
(P) $(0,0)$
(Q) $(3,0)$
(R) $(6,0)$
(S) $(12,0)$
questions.key_idea: With $y^2=4ax,\ a=3$: (A) midpoint is the focus $(a,0)$; (B) $K=(2a,0)$; (C) chords pass through $(4a,0)$; (D) the origin has equal power with respect to both circles.
solution: (A) The end of the latus rectum is $L(a,2a)=(3,6)$. Tangent: $6y=6(x+3)$, i.e. $x-y+3=0$, so $T(-3,0)$. Normal: $y-6=-1(x-3)$, i.e. $x+y-9=0$, so $G(9,0)$. Midpoint $=(3,0)$: Q.

(B) Let the chord through $K$ meet the parabola at $P(t),\ Q(t_1)$; then $K=(-att_1,0)$. The squares of the two parts are $KP^2=a^2t^2\left[(t+t_1)^2+4\right]$ and $KQ^2=a^2t_1^2\left[(t+t_1)^2+4\right]$.

$\frac1{KP^2}+\frac1{KQ^2}=\frac{t^2+t_1^2}{a^2t^2t_1^2\left[(t+t_1)^2+4\right]}=\frac{(t+t_1)^2-2tt_1}{a^2t^2t_1^2\left[(t+t_1)^2+4\right]}$, constant for every chord iff $-2tt_1=4$, i.e. $4+2tt_1=0$ and $tt_1=-2$.
(C) Let the chord be $y=mx+c$. Homogenising $y^2=12x$ with it: $cy^2=12x(y-mx)$, i.e. $cy^2-12xy+12mx^2=0$. The chords subtend a right angle at the origin: coefficient sum $c+12m=0$, so $c=-12m$.
The chord is $y=m(x-12)$: it passes through $(12,0)$: S.
(D) Let $AB$ pass through $E(c,0)$: $AB:\ 2x-(t_1+t_2)y+2at_1t_2=0$ gives $t_1t_2=-\frac ca$; similarly $t_3t_4=-\frac ca$ for $CD$.
Circle with $AB$ as diameter: $S_1:\ x^2+y^2-a(t_1^2+t_2^2)x-2a(t_1+t_2)y+c^2-4ac=0$. Circle with $CD$ as diameter: $S_2:\ x^2+y^2-a(t_3^2+t_4^2)x-2a(t_3+t_4)y+c^2-4ac=0$.
The radical axis $S_1-S_2=0$ has no constant term, so it passes through $(0,0)$: P.
questions.correction_note: Two lines of the PDF's working in (B) and (D) are grey boxes (missing images); the visible steps are kept and the hidden ones restored.

alternate_solutions.idea: (A) the tangent and normal at the latus-rectum end meet the axis at $(-a,0)$ and $(3a,0)$; (C) use $t_1t_2=-4$; (D) the power of the origin with respect to a circle on $AB$ as diameter is $\vec{OA}\cdot\vec{OB}$.
solution: (A) For the end $(a,2a)$ of the latus rectum, the tangent meets the axis at $(-a,0)=(-3,0)$ and the normal at $(3a,0)=(9,0)$; midpoint $(a,0)=(3,0)$: Q.
(B) Let the chord through $K(h,0)$ make an angle $\varphi$ with the axis: points $K+r(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$ give $r^2\sin^2\varphi-4a\cos\varphi\,r-4ah=0$.
(C) $OA\perp OB$: the slopes of $OA,OB$ are $\frac{2}{t_1},\frac{2}{t_2}$, so $\frac{4}{t_1t_2}=-1$ and $t_1t_2=-4$; the chord meets the axis at $(-at_1t_2,0)=(4a,0)=(12,0)$: S.
(D) The power of $O$ with respect to the circle on diameter $AB$ is $\vec{OA}\cdot\vec{OB}=a^2t_1^2t_2^2+4a^2t_1t_2=c^2-4ac$, the same for the circle on $CD$ (since $t_3t_4=-\frac ca$ too).
So $O$ has equal power with respect to both circles and lies on their radical axis: P.

useful_results: $y^2=4ax$: tangent and normal at the end of the latus rectum meet the axis at $(-a,0)$ and $(3a,0)$; their midpoint is the focus.
Chords through $K(h,0)$ with $\frac1{KP^2}+\frac1{KQ^2}$ constant exist only for $K=(2a,0)$, where the constant is $\frac{1}{4a^2}$.
All chords of $y^2=4ax$ subtending a right angle at the vertex pass through $(4a,0)$; at a general point $(x_0,y_0)$ of the curve they pass through $(x_0+4a,-y_0)$.
The radical axis of the circles on two chords through a common point $E$ of the axis passes through the vertex (the power of the vertex is $x_1x_2+y_1y_2=c^2-4ac$ for every chord through $(c,0)$).

questions.question:
Match the properties given in Column I with the corresponding curves given in Column II.
Column I
(A) The curve such that the product of the distances of any of its tangents from two given points is constant, can be
(B) A curve for which the length of the subnormal at any of its points is equal to $2$ and the curve passes through $(1,2)$, can be
(C) A curve passes through $(1,4)$ and is such that the segment joining any point $P$ on the curve and the point of intersection of the normal at $P$ with the $x$-axis is bisected by the $y$-axis. The curve can be
(D) A curve passes through $(1,2)$ and is such that the length of the normal at any of its points is equal to $2$. The curve can be
Column II
(P) Circle
(Q) Parabola
(R) Ellipse
(S) Hyperbola
questions.key_idea: (A) $p_1p_2=b^2$ holds for ellipse and hyperbola; (B) $y\frac{dy}{dx}=2$; (C) $2x+y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$; (D) $y^2\left(1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right)=4$.
solution: (A) The product of the perpendiculars from the two foci on any tangent of an ellipse or a hyperbola is the constant $b^2$ ($p_1p_2=b^2$): the curve can be an ellipse (R) or a hyperbola (S).
(B) Subnormal $=y\frac{dy}{dx}=2$, so $\frac{y^2}{2}=2x+C$. At $(1,2)$: $2=2+C$, so $C=0$ and $y^2=4x$: a parabola (Q).

(C) Normal at $P(x,y)$ with $m=\frac{dy}{dx}$: $Y-y=-\frac1m(X-x)$. With $Y=0$: $X=x+my$. The segment from $P$ to $G(x+my,0)$ is bisected by the $y$-axis, so the $x$-coordinates add to zero: $x+(x+my)=0$.
So $2x+y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$, i.e. $2x\,dx+y\,dy=0$, and $x^2+\frac{y^2}{2}=C$. It passes through $(1,4)$: $1+8=C=9$.

$m^2=\frac{4-y^2}{y^2}$, so $y\frac{dy}{dx}=\pm\sqrt{4-y^2}$ and $-\sqrt{4-y^2}=\pm x+C$. Taking the sign for which the curve passes through $(1,2)$: $-\sqrt{4-y^2}=x+C$ with $x=1,\ y=2$ gives $C=-1$.
questions.correction_note: In (D) the PDF writes 'x = 1, y = 4 => C = -1' but the curve passes through (1, 2); with (1, 2) the constant is C = -1, which is what it uses afterwards. Corrected the point. (In (C) the PDF's 'Y = y - ...' hidden line is not needed.) Answers unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise each curve by its standard property: constant subnormal $\Rightarrow$ parabola ($2a=2$); constant normal length $\Rightarrow$ circle of that radius; (C) the normal passes through $(-x,0)$.
solution: (B) For $y^2=4ax$ the subnormal is the constant $2a$. Subnormal $2$ means $a=1$; $y^2=4x$ passes through $(1,2)$. Parabola (Q).

(D) The normal of a circle is a radius, so its length is the radius: a circle of radius $2$ centred on the $x$-axis, $(x-c)^2+y^2=4$, through $(1,2)$ gives $(1-c)^2+4=4$, $c=1$: $(x-1)^2+y^2=4$. Circle (P).
(C) The $y$-axis bisects $P(x,y)$ and $G(x_G,0)$ iff $x_G=-x$: the normal at $P$ passes through $(-x,0)$, so its slope is $\frac{y}{2x}$ and the tangent slope is $-\frac{2x}{y}$.
(A) $p_1p_2=b^2$ for the ellipse and the hyperbola, so (R) and (S).

useful_results: Foci of an ellipse or hyperbola: the product of the perpendiculars on any tangent is $b^2$; conversely a constant product from two points gives a central conic.
Subnormal $y\frac{dy}{dx}$ is constant $=2a$ for a parabola $y^2=4ax$; subtangent is $2x$.
Length of the normal $=|y|\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$; a constant normal length $R$ gives circles of radius $R$ centred on the $x$-axis.
The $y$-axis bisecting $PG$ ($G$ on the $x$-axis) forces $G=(-x,0)$, so the normal passes through $(-x,0)$.

questions.question:
Consider the ellipse $ rac{x^2}{25}+ rac{y^2}{9}=1$ with centre $C$ and a point $P$ on it with eccentric angle $ rac\pi4$. The normal drawn at $P$ intersects the major and minor axes in $A$ and $B$ respectively. $N_1$ and $N_2$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from the foci $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively on the tangent at $P$ and $N$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the centre of the ellipse on the normal at $P$. The tangent at $P$ intersects the axis of $x$ at $T$. Match the entries of Column I with the entries of Column II.
Column I
(A) $(CA)(CT)$ is equal to
(B) $(PN)(PB)$ is equal to
(C) $(S_1N_1)(S_2N_2)$ is equal to
(D) $(S_1P)(S_2P)$ is equal to
Column II
(P) $9$
(Q) $16$
(R) $17$
(S) $25$
solution: (The ellipse and the eccentric angle are grey boxes in the PDF; $\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1$ and $\theta=\frac\pi4$ are recovered from the printed values $a^2-b^2=16$, $a^2=25$, $b^2=9$ and $a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2\cos^2\theta=17$.) Here $a=5$, $b=3$.

(A) The normal at $P(a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)$ meets the major axis at $A\left(\frac{a^2-b^2}{a}\cos\theta,0\right)$ and the tangent meets it at $T\left(\frac{a}{\cos\theta},0\right)$. $(CA)(CT)=a^2-b^2=16$: Q.
(C) The product of the focal perpendiculars on a tangent: $(S_1N_1)(S_2N_2)=b^2=9$: P.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's ellipse, the eccentric angle and the opening line of (A) are grey boxes (missing images). They were recovered from the printed values (a^2-b^2=16, a^2=25, b^2=9, and 17 = a^2 sin^2 t + b^2 cos^2 t, which gives sin^2 t = 1/2, t = pi/4); the working is otherwise the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Evaluate each product directly at $P\left(\frac5{\sqrt2},\frac3{\sqrt2}\right)$ from coordinates.
solution: $P=\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt2},\frac3{\sqrt2}\right)$. Tangent: $\frac{x}{5\sqrt2}+\frac{y}{3\sqrt2}=1$, i.e. $3x+5y=15\sqrt2$, so $T=(5\sqrt2,0)$. Normal: $5\sqrt2x-3\sqrt2y=16$, so $A=\left(\frac{16}{5\sqrt2},0\right)$ and $B=\left(0,-\frac{16}{3\sqrt2}\right)$.
(C) Foci $(\pm4,0)$: distances to $3x+5y-15\sqrt2=0$ are $\frac{|12-15\sqrt2|}{\sqrt{34}}$ and $\frac{|12+15\sqrt2|}{\sqrt{34}}$; product $=\frac{450-144}{34}=9$: P.

useful_results: Normal at $\theta$ meets the major axis at $\left(\frac{a^2-b^2}{a}\cos\theta,0\right)$ and the minor axis at $\left(0,-\frac{a^2-b^2}{b}\sin\theta\right)$; tangent meets the major axis at $\left(\frac{a}{\cos\theta},0\right)$: so $CA\cdot CT=a^2-b^2$.
For the normal at $P$: $PN\cdot PB=a^2$ and $PN\cdot PA=b^2$ hold for any point $P$ ($N$ the foot of the perpendicular from the centre, $A,B$ the axis intercepts of the normal).
Focal perpendiculars on a tangent: $S_1N_1\cdot S_2N_2=b^2$.
Focal radii: $S_1P=a+ex_P$ and $S_2P=a-ex_P$, whose product is $a^2-e^2x_P^2=a^2\sin^2\theta+b^2\cos^2\theta$.

concepts: Standard descriptions of a circle, parabola, ellipse and hyperbola (loci, parametric forms, eccentricity)
Locus of a point in the complex plane (focal definitions)
questions.question:
Match the conics in Column I with the statements / expressions in Column II. [JEE-2009]
Column I
(A) Circle
(B) Parabola
(C) Ellipse
(D) Hyperbola
Column II
(P) The locus of the point $(h,k)$ for which the line $hx+ky=1$ touches the circle $x^2+y^2=4$
(Q) Points $z$ in the complex plane satisfying $|z+2|-|z-2|=\pm3$
(R) Points of the conic have parametric representation $x=\sqrt3\left( rac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}ight),\ y= rac{2t}{1+t^2}$
(S) The eccentricity of the conic lies in the interval $1\le x<\infty$
(T) Points $z$ in the complex plane satisfying $\mathrm{Re}(z+1)^2=|z|^2+1$
questions.key_idea: (P) is the circle $h^2+k^2=\frac14$, (Q) a hyperbola, (R) the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{3}+y^2=1$, (T) the parabola $y^2=x$, and (S) holds for parabola and hyperbola.
solution: (P) $hx+ky=1$ touches $x^2+y^2=4$: the distance of the line from the origin is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}=2$, so $h^2+k^2=\frac14$: a circle. (A) - P.
(Q) $\left||z+2|-|z-2|\right|=3$: the difference of the distances from $(\pm2,0)$ is the constant $3<4$: a hyperbola.
(R) $x=\sqrt3\left(\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\right),\ y=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$. Put $t=\tan\theta$: $x=\sqrt3\cos2\theta$, $y=\sin2\theta$, so $\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+y^2=1$: an ellipse. (C) - R.
(S) The eccentricity lies in $[1,\infty)$ for a parabola ($e=1$) or a hyperbola ($e>1$).
Hence (A) - P; (B) - S, T; (C) - R; (D) - Q, S.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's solution for (P) and the parametric form in (R) of the question text are partly grey boxes; (R)'s expression is visible in its own solution, and (P) was restored.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise (Q) and (R) without trigonometry: focal difference $3<4$; and $\left(1-t^2\right)^2+(2t)^2=\left(1+t^2\right)^2$ gives $\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+y^2=1$ directly.
solution: (R) $\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+y^2=\frac{(1-t^2)^2+4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=\frac{(1+t^2)^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=1$: an ellipse, with no angle substitution.
(Q) $\left||z+2|-|z-2|\right|=3$ is the focal-difference definition with foci $\pm2$ (distance $4$) and $2a=3<4$: a hyperbola, $e=\frac43>1$.
(T) $\mathrm{Re}(z+1)^2=(x+1)^2-y^2$ and $|z|^2+1=x^2+y^2+1$ give $y^2=x$, a parabola: it has $e=1$, so (S) applies; similarly the hyperbola has $e>1$.
Matches: (A) P; (B) S, T; (C) R; (D) Q, S.

useful_results: Line $hx+ky=1$ touches $x^2+y^2=r^2$ iff $h^2+k^2=\frac{1}{r^2}$.
$\left||z-z_1|-|z-z_2|\right|=2a$ is a hyperbola iff $2a<|z_1-z_2|$; $|z-z_1|+|z-z_2|=2a$ is an ellipse iff $2a>|z_1-z_2|$.
Rational parametrisation $x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\ y=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$ traces the unit circle (all of it except $(-1,0)$); scaling $x$ by $\sqrt3$ gives an ellipse.
$\mathrm{Re}(z+k)^2=|z|^2+c$ reduces to a parabola because the $x^2$ and $y^2$ coefficients cancel except for one variable.
